# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Exposure-bounded atovaquone induces DHODH-dependent maturation in salvage-poor cytarabine-residual AML through complex III inhibition and oxidized-ubiquinone restriction before ATP failure

Hypothesis. In cytarabine-surviving AML with inadequate pyrimidine salvage, atovaquone will partially inhibit complex III, restrict oxidized ubiquinone and DHODH flux, and induce maturation of initially immature leukemic cells before energetic failure, reducing leukemia propagation. NPM1-mutant AML is a prespecified genotype restriction, not an evidence-supported responder biomarker. The ATP-sparing window and normal-cell advantage are speculative bridges.

Supported premises. Cytarabine-resistant cells required oxidative metabolism in studied models but were not consistently enriched for leukemia stem cells [S2]. Separately, DHODH inhibition promoted differentiation in experimental AML [S4]. Neither establishes DHODH dependence in oxidative survivors. Functionally assessed ROS-low leukemia-stem-cell fractions remain a separate benchmark [S1]. Venetoclax–azacitidine supplies an established metabolic comparator, not the repurposing proposal [S3].

Unverified prior knowledge requiring confirmation: atovaquone is approved for Pneumocystis pneumonia treatment/prevention and, with proguanil, malaria. Its high protein binding and mammalian complex-III potency are not verified here. Human DHODH uses oxidized ubiquinone; uridine salvage and respiratory-independent yeast URA1 can bypass pyrimidine restriction. These biochemical recollections and drug-specific exposure assumptions are not packet findings.

Exposure-first testing. Verify approved-dose pharmacokinetics and binding; calculate Cu(t)=fu(t)×Ctotal(t). Reproduce measured free concentration–time profiles in protein-containing cultures of three independently generated, same-stratum residual-state models. Quantify complex-III inhibition, ubiquinone redox, dihydroorotate:orotate, isotope-traced pyrimidine flux, UTP, ATP, and total ATP-production rate. Prespecify a window with at least 30% UTP depletion while ATP and ATP-production rate remain at least 80% of vehicle, preceding maturation. No window rejects the temporal claim; no clinically reproducible exposure duration stops repurposing. Free plasma Cmax alone is insufficient: effective-duration marrow exposure must subsequently be demonstrated.

Context gates are fixed before testing atovaquone response. Select NPM1-mutant cytarabine-pulse/washout survivors with at least 80% immature genotype-positive cells, defined by CD11b/CD14 negativity and blast morphology. Require biomass-normalized respiration and isotope-confirmed fatty-acid oxidation at least 1.5-fold cycling-matched normal CD34-positive cells, with elevation versus paired pretreatment blasts. These are operational thresholds, not packet-derived cutoffs. Confirm fatty-acid-oxidation attribution genetically rather than through inhibitor sensitivity alone; record proliferation. Define inadequate salvage by failure to maintain UTP during partial reference-DHODH blockade across verified physiological pyrimidine availability—not high de novo flux alone. Measure normal-cell DHODH/salvage flux and colony dose responses in parallel; report the observed therapeutic index without presuming selectivity.

Mechanistic discrimination. Isolated assays must establish complex-III inhibition without direct DHODH inhibition. Include a biochemically validated direct DHODH inhibitor and cytarabine-only controls. Primary specimens receive targeted UTP/redox measurements, nontoxic supraphysiological uridine rescue, and longitudinal single-cell tracking from index-sorted immature cells, with terminal genotype confirmation, morphology, absolute mature/immature counts, apoptosis and washout clonogenicity. Physiological pyrimidine availability determines eligibility; supraphysiological uridine tests bypass. Induce URA1 only after establishing the residual state in an engineered line passing exposure/timing gates—not in scarce primary blasts. Validate both bypasses against the direct inhibitor through recovery of pyrimidine pools and phenotypes; bypass need not normalize dihydroorotate:orotate. Rescues must restore pools without reversing complex-III inhibition.

If these tests pass, cytarabine-primed xenografts test duration-matched marrow exposure and pharmacodynamics, normal hematopoietic recovery, and a prespecified threefold reduction in viability-normalized, post-washout limiting-dilution secondary-transplant initiating frequency. Differentiation and initiating-cell loss are distinct endpoints. Validated uridine/URA1 bypass restoring pyrimidines while atovaquone-induced maturation and clonogenic loss persist, despite persistent respiratory inhibition, falsifies the proposed mediation—even if atovaquone remains cytotoxic. Comparable normal-progenitor injury rejects selective utility.

Alternatives include preferential survival of pre-existing mature cells, delayed cytarabine injury, direct DHODH binding and generalized energetic toxicity; fate tracking, washout controls, enzyme assays and kinetics distinguish these explanations. Protein binding, marrow pyrimidine availability, species differences and genotype restriction limit translation; maturation need not imply durable clearance. Novelty remains unverified: a prior ETC–DHODH differentiation result would negate pathway novelty, while an atovaquone report demonstrating this same exposure-timed, salvage-defined residual-cell mechanism would retire the incremental claim. Neither result can be identified from this packet.

Ranked proposal:
Exposure-bounded atovaquone induces DHODH-dependent maturation in salvage-poor cytarabine-residual AML through complex III inhibition and oxidized-ubiquinone restriction before ATP failure
